segments.t: In Gabriel's quiet office, senior agent Arlette Azemar checks in on her colleague as he wrestles with private doubts. Confessing his jealousy over Sofia's new artistic project with Julien Dore, Gabriel receives wise and reassuring advice from the veteran agent. Listen to the scene in French first. Don't worry about catching every word.
Tu vas bien, mon cher Gabriel?
C'est super pour le film de Sofia.
Depuis leur rencontre, Sofia est rayonnante.
Je crois que je suis jaloux!
Je ne suis plus si sûr.
Le scénario est un peu vulgaire.
Tu connais très bien ce métier.
On vend du désir au cinéma.
Julien aime beaucoup les jolies femmes.
Je ne veux pas d'histoire.
Il faut du désir entre artistes.
Laisse-la vivre sa propre vie.
Fais-lui confiance avant tout.
Elle t'aimera encore plus ainsi.
Now let's break down the scene step by step. Listen to each line, followed by its meaning and a short explanation.
Tu vas bien, mon cher Gabriel?
'Are you doing well, my dear Gabriel?' Adding 'my dear' ahead of Gabriel's name gives Arlette's casual 'you go well?' a warm maternal touch in French.
C'est super pour le film de Sofia.
'It is great for Sofia's movie.' French has no apostrophe-'s' possessive, saying 'the film of Sofia' instead, led here by casual 'super'.
Depuis leur rencontre, Sofia est rayonnante.
'Since their meeting, Sofia is radiant.' Built on 'ray' or 'beam of light', that glowing final word sounds its 't' when describing Sofia in French.
Je crois que je suis jaloux!
'I think that I am jealous!' Notice 'jealous' ends on a silent 'x' in French for Gabriel, whereas for a female speaker it shifts to a 'z' sound.
Je ne suis plus si sûr.
'I am no longer so sure.' Swapping 'not' for the word meaning 'more' after 'am' flips the negative meaning to 'no longer' in French.
Le scénario est un peu vulgaire.
'The script is a bit vulgar.' Softening the cognate 'vulgar' with a handy chunk meaning 'a little' makes Gabriel's excuse sound hesitant.
Tu connais très bien ce métier.
'You know this business very well.' That final word names a craft or profession you practice — closer to 'line of work' than corporate 'business'.
On vend du désir au cinéma.
'We sell desire in cinema.' Abstract qualities sold in unspecified amounts take 'of the' before 'desire' in French, followed by 'at the cinema'.
Julien aime beaucoup les jolies femmes.
'Julien likes pretty women a lot.' With people, adding 'a lot' right after 'love' tones it down to 'likes a lot' rather than romantic love in French.
Je ne veux pas d'histoire.
'I do not want any trouble.' In the negative, 'some' shifts to shortened 'of' before 'story', which here idiomatically means 'drama' or 'trouble'.
Il faut du désir entre artistes.
'There must be desire between artists.' Opening with impersonal 'it is necessary' plus 'some desire' expresses general artistic need in French.
Laisse-la vivre sa propre vie.
'Let her live her own life.' Placed ahead of 'life', that describing word means 'own', whereas placed after something in French it means 'clean'.
Fais-lui confiance avant tout.
'Trust her above all.' Built as 'make-to-her trust', this key expression closes with 'before all' to mean 'above all else'.
Elle t'aimera encore plus ainsi.

'She will love you even more that way.' Pairing 'still' with 'more' creates 'even more' in French, wrapped up neatly by a formal word meaning 'thus'. Now let's listen to the whole exchange once more from beginning to end.
Tu vas bien, mon cher Gabriel?
C'est super pour le film de Sofia.
Depuis leur rencontre, Sofia est rayonnante.
Je crois que je suis jaloux!
Je ne suis plus si sûr.
Le scénario est un peu vulgaire.
Tu connais très bien ce métier.
On vend du désir au cinéma.
Julien aime beaucoup les jolies femmes.
Je ne veux pas d'histoire.
Il faut du désir entre artistes.
Laisse-la vivre sa propre vie.
Fais-lui confiance avant tout.
Elle t'aimera encore plus ainsi.
Calmed by Arlette's experience and warmth, Gabriel learns to separate his professional role from his personal insecurities. See you next time!
Bonne journée!
